learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected $60 and locked the best first-price bid prediction for an $80 value against one rival bidding half of a uniform $0 to $100 value.
observations.exploration: Initial $80 bid had certain win and zero profit. Tested $60: certain win, $20 profit; $50: certain win, $30; $40: 80% win, $40 kept, $32 expected. Then tested $20: 40% win, $60 kept, $24 expected.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to $40 and explained the flat win probability above $50, then two percentage points of lost win chance per dollar below it. It identified $40 as the best tradeoff and qualified the equilibrium with one uniform-value rival.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot at $40. A dashed expected-profit curve peaked at the highlighted $32 point above $40, with visited $50, $60 and $80 points. Win chance, conditional gain and expected profit were separately labelled.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884163 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The question requires balancing likelihood and gain rather than only winning.

interaction.reason: Preset and free slider bids expose both sides of the optimum.
interaction.evidence: Expected profit rose to $32 at $40 then fell to $24 at $20.

payoff.reason: The reveal explains the observed kink and optimum under explicit assumptions.
payoff.evidence: Win chance stays certain through $50, then falls as bids decrease.

clarity.reason: Separate readouts distinguish conditional gain from expectation.

transfer.reason: The bidding rule is explained within the original fixed setup without a new case.
transfer.evidence: Neither valuation nor rival strategy changes.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: Winning less often can yield greater average profit.
surprise.evidence: $40 earns more in expectation than a certain-win $50 bid.

visualExplanation.reason: The curve and three readouts reveal the tradeoff.
visualExplanation.evidence: The visited lower $20 bid lies below the profit peak.

playfulness.reason: A slider allows probing beyond the offered candidates.
playfulness.evidence: The $20 test checks the other side of the maximum.

practicalValue.reason: It clarifies why first-price bidders shade below value.
practicalValue.evidence: The result is explicitly conditional on the rival model.

depth.reason: The lesson connects win probability, surplus and optimal response.
depth.evidence: It explains the different behavior above and below the rival's maximum bid.

complexity.reason: The controls are simple, but expectation and strategic assumptions require careful interpretation.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Moderate: multiply probability by gain and compare opposing effects.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low: presets and a bid slider.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: Maximum chance of winning does not maximize expected surplus.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: First-price bidding and equilibrium strategy are introduced.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Moderate: profit curve, probability and dollar readouts.

whyCool: Giving up some wins can pay more because the wins you keep become more valuable.
caveat: One rival's fixed uniform-value half-bid strategy determines this optimum; it is not universal auction advice.
missingEvidence: No fresh valuation or rival strategy was tested.
